**Problem.** Find all $f:(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ with $f(f(xy)+2xy)=3xf(y)+3yf(x)$ for all $x,y>0$.

**Claim.** The unique solution is $f(x)=4x$.

**Verification.** $f(f(xy)+2xy)=f(4xy+2xy)=f(6xy)=24xy$ and $3xf(y)+3yf(x)=3x\cdot4y+3y\cdot4x=24xy$. ✓

**Proof of uniqueness.**

Let $P(x,y)$ denote the assertion and set $c:=f(1)>0$.

*Step 1: Reducing the dependence on $xy$.* Fix $t>0$ and consider $x,y>0$ with $xy=t$. The left-hand side $f(f(t)+2t)$ depends only on $t$, hence so does the right-hand side:
$$x\,f(y)+y\,f(x)=C(t)\quad\text{whenever }xy=t.$$
Setting $x=t,\,y=1$ gives $C(t)=t\,f(1)+f(t)=tc+f(t)$.

Writing $y=t/x$ and dividing by $t$: $\dfrac{x}{t}f\!\left(\dfrac{t}{x}\right)+\dfrac{f(x)}{x}\cdot\dfrac{1}{1}=c+\dfrac{f(t)}{t}$, i.e. with $F(x):=f(x)/x$,
$$F(t/x)+F(x)=c+F(t).\qquad(\star)$$
Substituting $a=x,\ b=t/x$ (so $t=ab$): $F(b)+F(a)=c+F(ab)$, i.e.
$$F(ab)=F(a)+F(b)-c.$$
Defining $G(x):=F(x)-c$, we obtain the multiplicative Cauchy equation
$$G(ab)=G(a)+G(b),\qquad x>0,$$
and $f(x)=x\bigl(c+G(x)\bigr)$. Since $f(x)>0$ for all $x>0$,
$$G(x)>-c\quad\text{for all }x>0.\qquad(\star\star)$$

*Step 2: Forcing $G\equiv 0$.* Suppose $G$ is not identically zero; pick $a>0$ with $G(a)\ne 0$. If $G(a)>0$, then $G(a^{-n})=-n\,G(a)\to-\infty$, contradicting $(\star\star)$ for large $n$. If $G(a)<0$, then $G(a^{n})=n\,G(a)\to-\infty$, again contradicting $(\star\star)$. Hence $G\equiv 0$, so $f(x)=cx$.

*Step 3: Determining $c$.* Substituting $f(x)=cx$ into the original equation:
$$\text{LHS}=f(cxy+2xy)=c(c+2)xy,\qquad \text{RHS}=3x\cdot cy+3y\cdot cx=6c\,xy.$$
Thus $c(c+2)=6c$, i.e. $c(c-4)=0$. Since $c>0$, we get $c=4$.

Therefore $f(x)=4x$ is the unique solution.
